newsitem.title: UK: NATO will scale down Bosnia peace force next year.
newsitem.headline: NATO will scale down Bosnia peace force next year.

text.p: NATO said on Wednesday it was ready to send troops to Bosnia for another 18 months but made clear it planned to cut down the size of the 30,000-strong contingent at regular intervals during its mission.

NATO Secretary General Javier Solana said the North Atlantic alliance planned to review the size of its international peacekeeping force in Bosnia next June and December with a view to reducing it substantially over 1997.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's new Stabilisation Force (SFOR) is due later this month to take over from the current peace force, IFOR, which is twice its size.

Solana told an international conference on Bosnia in London: "We are planning for an 18-month mission, to be reviewed at six and 12 months, with a view to progressively reducing the forces' presence to a deterrent posture and eventually withdrawal."
The conference attended by 50 foreign ministers has been called to review progress in the 12 months since the signing of the Dayton peace accord, which ended 43 months of war in Bosnia.

The talks have been overshadowed by mass demonstrations in Belgrade by opponents of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, the Balkan strongman on whom the West has relied heavily to deliver the peace in Bosnia.

Thousands of students and supporters of opposition parties have marched through the Serbian capital for the past two weeks, calling for Milosevic's resignation on grounds of alleged ballot rigging in local elections.
U.S. President Bill Clinton announced plans for an 18-month tour of duty for SFOR shortly after his re-election last month.

Junior British Foreign Office minister Nicholas Bonsor told a parliamentary committee last month that Washington's allies had been surprised by the statement as they expected SFOR to be in Bosnia for just one year.
A British diplomat said on Wednesday: "We would expect a substantial drawdown for the final six months."

Britain has committed itself to contributing a heavily armed contingent of 5,000 troops to SFOR. NATO sources said the German government, which has said it will send troops to Bosnia, was concerned at the prospect of an 18 month mission there.
Solana said that in 1997 the emphasis should move away from soldiers enforcing peace to Bosnian politicians encouraging it.
"The political and civil aspects of peace implementation must take a more prominent role over the miliary aspects," he said.

He told delegates from Bosnia: "We are prepared to commit our soldiers and our resources for another 18 months, but expect you to commit yourselves -- in deeds as well as words -- to making the peace endure."
